query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a uniaxial compressive stress during rapid thermal annealing of pure, equiatomic FeCoNi thin films will induce anisotropic lattice distortions that favor the formation of low‐symmetry (possibly L1₀-like) chemically ordered domains, thereby increasing magnetic coercivity relative to unstressed, conventionally annealed films.
generation.material_initial_state: Pure, equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy in a disordered face-centered cubic (fcc) phase exhibiting high saturation magnetization and very low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) performed under an imposed uniaxial compressive stress (i.e., stress-annealing) applied during the thermal treatment.
generation.conditions: Thin films of sputtered FeCoNi on substrates that allow or transmit compressive stress (e.g., flexible or specially designed rigid substrates with external loading). RTA parameters set to ~350°C for 15–30 seconds in a controlled atmosphere (vacuum or inert gas) with an applied uniaxial stress in the range of tens of MPa.
generation.structural_mediator: The applied compressive stress is expected to induce anisotropic lattice distortions during rapid heating, thereby driving directional atomic rearrangements that lower the effective lattice symmetry and potentially nucleate chemically ordered domains (analogous to L1₀ ordering) within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: The combination of thermal energy from rapid annealing and imposed uniaxial compressive stress promotes a non-isotropic atomic diffusion pathway. This pathway reduces the crystallographic symmetry and enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy, which increases domain wall pinning. The engineered low-symmetry ordered regions are expected to act as structural obstacles for domain wall motion, thereby enhancing coercivity without markedly sacrificing the high saturation magnetization of the parent phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline of conventionally RTA-treated pure FeCoNi films (with very low coercivity), the stress-assisted RTA process will produce films with a significantly higher coercivity (by a factor that may exceed the increase achieved by annealing alone) while maintaining similar high saturation magnetization. The improvement is attributed solely to processing-induced chemical ordering and anisotropic strain.
generation.baseline: Pure equiatomic FeCoNi films undergoing standard rapid thermal annealing without the application of any directional mechanical stress.
generation.boundary: The expectation applies to nearly equiatomic, high configurational entropy FeCoNi thin films processed under conditions that preserve the overall fcc structure while allowing the nucleation of low-symmetry ordered domains. The effectiveness of the stress-induced ordering may be limited to thin-film geometries and may not directly translate to bulk samples.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from RTA-induced phase transformations in multicomponent HEAs (PMC11426066 evidence) and the role of anisotropic strain in enhancing magnetic anisotropy to a pure FeCoNi system, which has not been previously tested. The exact magnitude of the coercivity enhancement and the extent of induced ordering remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of sputtered equiatomic FeCoNi thin films on substrates designed for stress application. Subject one set to RTA under a defined uniaxial compressive stress (e.g., 30–50 MPa) and the other set to identical RTA conditions without applied stress. Characterize both sets using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to probe for any evidence of induced low-symmetry or chemically ordered domains. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) to determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: XRD for detection of any symmetry lowering or superlattice reflections
TEM for observing atomic ordering and grain structure modifications
VSM for hysteresis loop evaluation (coercivity, saturation magnetization)
Optional strain mapping techniques to quantify induced lattice distortion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-assisted RTA films do not show a statistically significant increase (e.g., >10% higher) in coercivity compared to the control films and no clear evidence of induced low-symmetry chemical ordering is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

While the combination of saturation magnetization and coercivity for these RTA‐ treated FeCoNiMnCu films is impressive in comparison to previously reported bulk systems, the coercivity is still modest, due to the high symmetry of the cubic lattice which limits the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The facilitation of low‐symmetry chemical order and crystal structure combined with strong spin‐orbit coupling is in general necessary to realize strong magnetocrysalline anisotropy. To achieve these conditions in a high entropy system, we have added 50 at.% Pt to the FeCoNiMnCu alloy, employing the high entropy intermetallic design approach in search of highly anisotropic L10 ordering. Although the certainty of Pt sites reduces the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, we demonstrate below that such optimized entropy can still stabilize a single high‐entropy L10 phase.
